chapters.title: Chapter 1: Why Machine Learning for Trading Is Different

lessons.title: From Quant Factors to Learned Signals: Where ML Fits in a Systematic Pipeline

body.text: Machine learning is not a replacement for the factor framework you already know. Most of the time it is a smarter way to combine the same economically motivated signals, value, momentum, quality, and only sometimes is it a way to generate a primary signal that does not map to any single named factor at all. Confusing the two is how a genuinely useful upgrade turns into an unexplainable black box a risk committee will never approve.

children.text: The Systematic Pipeline You Already Know

A conventional quant equity pipeline runs in a straight line: pull raw price and fundamental data, construct named factors like value, momentum, and quality, convert each into a cross-sectional z-score against the rest of the universe, combine those z-scores into a single composite score, usually with fixed or slowly-adjusted weights, then rank, build the portfolio, and execute. Every step is transparent enough to explain to a risk committee in one sentence. Machine learning does not throw this pipeline away. It targets one or more specific steps in it, and knowing which step you are targeting is the single most important design decision in this course.

body.title: Three Eras of Systematic Equity Investing

events.title: Simple Screens
events.description: Fixed threshold rules, such as buying stocks below a certain P/E or price-to-book, with no formal combination logic across signals.

events.title: Linear Composite Scoring
events.description: Named, economically motivated factors (value, momentum, quality, low volatility) are z-scored and combined through a linear weighted average or a cross-sectional regression.

events.title: Learned Combination and Direct Prediction
events.description: Tree ensembles and neural networks either replace the linear combination step with a nonlinear one, or predict returns and probabilities directly from a wider feature set than a handful of named factors.

children.text: Where Machine Learning Actually Fits: Three Roles, Not One

In practice, ML shows up in a systematic Indian equity pipeline in one of three distinct roles. They use overlapping tools, the same random forest or gradient booster can serve any of them, but they answer completely different questions, and this course's Chapters 2 through 4 sit in different roles at different points.

Role 1: a smarter combination function. Instead of a fixed weighted average of value, momentum, and quality z-scores, a tree ensemble learns how those factors interact. A stock that is cheap and has improving return on equity behaves very differently from a stock that is cheap because its fundamentals are deteriorating, the classic value trap, and a linear model averaging the two z-scores cannot express that distinction. A tree-based model can split on "cheap AND improving quality" versus "cheap AND deteriorating quality" as genuinely different regions of the data, which is exactly what Chapter 2 builds.

body.text: The most useful early win from ML on a mature factor desk is rarely a brand new signal. It is usually a better way to combine the signals the desk already trusts, which is exactly why Role 1 is where most quant teams start.

children.text: Role 2: a primary signal generator. Here the model does not receive a small set of named factors as input. It receives a wider feature set, price and volume patterns, order flow proxies, cross-sectional rankings across many raw ratios, and learns to predict a return or a probability directly, without being told in advance that "value" or "momentum" is the right lens. This is where most of Chapter 2's momentum case study and all of Chapter 4's deep learning work sit. It can surface genuinely new structure, and it carries genuinely higher overfitting and interpretability risk, which is why this chapter spent an entire lesson on exactly that risk.

markDefs.definition: A secondary model that does not predict direction. It takes an existing primary signal (rule-based or ML-generated) and predicts whether to act on that specific bet and how large to size it, filtering out the primary signal's weakest calls.

children.text: Role 3: a filter on top of an existing signal, known as

. Here you keep a primary signal you already trust, a moving average crossover, a factor composite, anything, and train a second model only to answer "should I take this specific signal, and how much size," never "which direction." The next lesson builds this in full, including the triple-barrier labeling method it depends on.

body.title: Two Very Different Uses of the Same Toolkit

columns.label: ML as a Combination Layer (Role 1)
points: Sits on top of factors the desk already understands and can explain
Easier to sanity-check with SHAP, since inputs are named and economically motivated
Lower data requirement; fewer, cleaner features
A defensible, incremental upgrade to an existing pipeline

columns.label: ML as a Primary Signal Generator (Role 2)
points: Predicts return or probability directly from a wide feature set
Can capture structure no named factor was built to describe
Higher overfitting risk; depends on the labeling and validation discipline from this chapter
Harder to explain to a risk desk without SHAP-based interpretation

children.text: The Data Layer: What Feeds an Indian Systematic ML Pipeline

Whichever role you build for, the pipeline starts with the same data layer. Price and volume history comes from NSE and BSE feeds, either exchange bhavcopy files or a paid vendor. Fundamental data for value and quality factors can come from an institutional vendor, or, for a smaller desk or an individual researcher, from a source like screener.in, which standardizes ratios across thousands of listed Indian companies. Corporate actions, splits, bonuses, dividends, need to be adjusted for before any of it touches a model. Once a model produces a signal, execution for a prop desk or a scaling systematic trader typically runs through a broker API such as Zerodha's Kite Connect.

body.label: screener.in
body.description: A widely used, accessible source for standardized Indian company fundamentals and ratios, useful for building factor and ML feature datasets without an institutional data vendor subscription.

body.label: Zerodha Kite Connect
body.description: A broker API commonly used by Indian prop desks and scaling systematic traders to route orders programmatically once a model's signal has been generated.

markDefs.definition: The distortion introduced when a historical dataset only includes entities that still exist today, silently excluding companies that were delisted, went bankrupt, merged, or were dropped from an index along the way.

children.text: One data-layer mistake deserves a warning before you touch a single line of model code: building your historical universe only from today's index constituents. That silently introduces

, removing exactly the companies whose failure a good model should have learned to anticipate. A universe built this way will make every model trained on it, ML or otherwise, look better in backtest than it could ever have performed live.

body.text: If your historical Nifty 500 dataset was built by taking the current 500 constituents and pulling their full price history back to 2010, it is survivorship-biased. Names that were delisted, merged, or dropped from the index between 2010 and today are missing entirely, and they are disproportionately likely to be the ones a well-trained model would have flagged as risky.

children.text: Capacity and Liquidity: A Constraint No Feature Set Captures

F&O trading on the NSE is only available in a limited list of stocks, a list SEBI and the exchange revise periodically based on market-wide position limits and trading activity, not the full universe of listed names. Even in cash equities, impact cost rises quickly once you move from large caps into small and mid caps. None of this shows up in a typical feature set built from price, volume, and fundamentals. A model can rank a thinly traded small-cap counter as its top pick, with no idea that a desk trying to build a meaningful position in it would move the price against itself before the order finished filling.

body.label: Where Most Feature Sets Are Silent
body.context: A model scoring stocks purely on price, volume, and fundamentals has no idea whether a desk can actually build a meaningful position in the name it just ranked first, without moving the price against itself. Liquidity and capacity constraints belong in portfolio construction, downstream of the model, not inside it.

children.text: How This Course's Chapters Slot Into the Pipeline

The next two lessons finish this chapter's foundation: correct labeling and a working data toolkit. Chapters 2 and 3 build ensembles that mostly occupy Role 1, combining factors you already trust, though the Chapter 2 case study also shows Role 2 in action on raw momentum features. Chapter 4's deep learning work sits almost entirely in Role 2, learning directly from price sequences. Meta-labeling, Role 3, is not tied to any one chapter. It can wrap around a rule-based signal, a Chapter 2 ensemble, or a Chapter 4 neural network equally well, which is exactly why it gets its own lesson next rather than living inside any single model chapter.

body.title: Choosing a Role for ML on Your Desk
body.scenario: Your desk already runs a well-understood value-quality composite score on the Nifty 500, built as a simple weighted average of z-scored ratios pulled from screener.in-style fundamental data, rebalanced quarterly. Backtested Sharpe is decent, but your own manual review of past winners and losers suggests cheap-and-improving names behave very differently from cheap-and-deteriorating ones, a distinction the fixed linear weights cannot express.
body.prompt: Which of the three roles for ML described in this lesson fits this situation best, and why not the other two?
body.modelAnswer: This is a textbook case for ML as a combination layer, Role 1, not a primary signal generator or meta-labeling. The desk already has interpretable, economically motivated factors the risk committee understands and trusts; what is missing is a nonlinear combination function that can capture the interaction between value and the direction of quality change, something a simple weighted z-score average cannot express. A tree ensemble trained on the existing factor scores as inputs, with SHAP used to confirm it is genuinely learning a value-times-quality-trend interaction rather than overfitting, is a smaller and more defensible change than replacing the whole pipeline with a Role 2 primary signal generator trained on raw features, and it does not require the meta-labeling machinery from the next lesson, which is built for filtering a separate primary signal's bets, not for combining existing factors.

body.title: Spotting the Missing Piece
body.question: A research team builds an ML feature dataset for Nifty 500 stocks using only the current 500 constituents' full price history back to 2010, pulling fundamentals from a standard source. What is the most likely hidden flaw in this dataset before any model is even trained?
options: The dataset has too many features relative to observations
The dataset likely suffers from survivorship bias, since delisted or removed constituents are excluded
Fundamental data from a source like screener.in cannot be used for quantitative research
The 2010 start date makes the dataset too short for machine learning
body.explanation: Using only today's index constituents to build a historical dataset silently removes every company that was delisted, went bankrupt, merged, or was dropped from the index along the way, exactly the kind of company whose failure a good model should learn to anticipate. This survivorship bias makes backtested performance look better than any live version of the same pipeline would have achieved, and it has nothing to do with feature count, data source, or history length.

points: ML plays at least three distinct roles in a systematic pipeline: a nonlinear combination layer over factors you already trust, a primary signal generator learning from a wider feature set, and a meta-labeling filter that sizes bets from an existing signal
Choosing the right role matters more than choosing the right algorithm; the same tree ensemble is a defensible upgrade in one role and an unexplainable black box in another
Indian systematic pipelines commonly draw price and volume data from NSE and BSE feeds, fundamentals from sources like screener.in, and route execution through broker APIs like Zerodha's Kite Connect
A dataset built only from current index constituents carries survivorship bias and overstates backtested performance, regardless of model choice
F&O liquidity on the NSE is limited to a periodically revised list of stocks, and impact cost belongs in portfolio construction, downstream of the model, not inside it
This course's ensemble chapters mostly occupy the combination and primary-signal-generation roles; meta-labeling, covered next, wraps around either one
